hook_text: In July 1888, smoke filled the tunnels of the De Beers Mine. Most of the dead were black workers who had no way out.
clip_script: Kimberley started as an open hole. But the sides kept collapsing and water flooded the bottom. So the companies went underground: shafts, tunnels, dynamite and steam engines. Underground, the roof could fall at any moment. A charge that failed to fire could explode when a drill struck it. Deep down, the rock was hot and the air was thick with dust. In 1888, a fire filled the De Beers Mine with smoke, and about two hundred miners died. The heaviest, most dangerous work, drilling, shovelling, pushing trucks, was done by black migrant workers. The better jobs were kept for white workers by rules called the colour bar. On the gold mines, dust scarred miners' lungs. The tunnels made fortunes, and cost lives.
visual_style: A whiteboard cross-section of an open pit turning into shafts and tunnels, with icons for rockfall, dynamite, smoke and dust, and a split figure showing who drilled and who supervised.
pacing: Slow descent, quickening at the dangers, ending quietly.
